titre: A Starfish Invented a Word for Ecology
accroche: In 1963, a biologist removes starfish by hand from a patch of rock, twice a month, to see what would collapse.
contenu_vulgarise:
In June 1963, the ecologist Robert Paine picks a strip of rock eight meters by two at Mukkaw Bay, on the Olympic Peninsula in Washington State. Twice a month in spring and summer, once a month in winter, he goes back with a crowbar, pries off the purple sea stars, Pisaster ochraceus, clinging to the rock one by one, and throws them into the sea. On a neighboring stretch of shoreline, left untouched, he does nothing.

## What happens when you remove a single predator

Before the experiment, the portion of rock that is cleared of its starfish is home to fifteen species: mussels, barnacles, anemones, limpets, several algae. Pisaster feeds on a good share of them at once without completely eliminating any: a generalist predator, one that tastes everything rather than specializing in a single prey.

Three years later, in 1966, Paine publishes his results in The American Naturalist. Without the starfish, the mussel Mytilus californianus, the most competitive for the available space, invades the rock and crowds out almost everything else. The number of species on the plot falls to eight. On the control plot, nothing has changed.

The mechanism isn't hunger: Pisaster doesn't eat enough mussels to noticeably reduce their numbers. It eats enough to keep them from monopolizing the space. Removing a predator that weighs little in the ecosystem's total biomass was enough to change its composition almost entirely.

## A word for what Paine had just shown

In 1969, in a three-page note published in the same journal, Paine proposes a word for this kind of species: “keystone,” the central stone of an arch that, once removed, brings down the whole structure, even though it is only one stone among dozens. The term stuck, and it extends well beyond starfish: wolves, beavers, elephants, and sharks are now routinely called keystone species, with uneven success in demonstrating their effect as cleanly as Paine did on his rock.

## What the experiment doesn't say

An article revisiting the experiment in 2016 points out a nuance that the popular account often leaves aside. The mussel that invades the rock is not merely a conqueror that impoverishes everything: its dense mat serves as a three-dimensional habitat for more than three hundred other species, sponges, worms, small crustaceans, living lodged in the gaps of this carpet of shells. The diversity of organisms attached directly to the rock drops when Pisaster disappears. The total diversity of the system, though, goes up.

The story told most often, a predator removed, an ecosystem that collapses, is therefore not false. It simplifies a system in which the loss of one diversity hides another, harder to see from the rock, at human height.

repere.texte: On the same plot of rock, eight meters by two, cleared of its starfish twice a month for three years, the number of recorded species falls from fifteen to eight; on the control plot left untouched, none is missing.
repere.source: Paine, R.T., “Food Web Complexity and Species Diversity,” The American Naturalist, 100(910), 1966

carte.punch: Removing a single species, a minority one in the ecosystem, was enough to change its whole composition.
carte.idee: In 1963, the ecologist Robert Paine removes starfish by hand from a patch of rock in the United States. Within three years, the number of species living there falls from fifteen to eight. In 1969, he proposes the term “keystone species” for this predator, scarce but essential to the balance.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Ecologists Struggle to Get a Grip on 'Keystone Species'
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Quanta Magazine; on the sometimes fuzzy use today of the term coined by Paine.

quiz.question: Why can removing a species that weighs little in an ecosystem's total biomass change its whole composition?
choix: Because this species is actually the most numerous in the ecosystem, despite its low biomass
Because it limits a competitively dominant species that, left to itself, monopolizes the available space
Because its disappearance deprives the other species of their main food source
Because it is the only species able to reproduce in this environment
quiz.explication: Pisaster doesn't eat enough mussels to noticeably reduce their numbers: it eats enough to keep the competitively dominant mussel from invading all the available space. It isn't a matter of the predator's abundance or of a role as a food source, but of regulating a competition.

quiz_supplementaire.question: By what mechanism does removing Pisaster change the composition of the ecosystem, according to Paine's experiment?
choix: Pisaster doesn't eat enough of it to reduce its numbers, but enough to keep it from monopolizing the space
The mucus secreted by Pisaster repels the other predators on the rock
Pisaster fertilizes the rock with its waste, which favors algae
Pisaster breaks the mussels' shells so that other species can feed on them
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text states that the mechanism isn't hunger: Pisaster doesn't eat enough mussels to reduce their numbers, but enough to keep them from monopolizing the space.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the 2016 reanalysis by Lafferty and Suchanek reveal about Paine's experiment?
choix: That the original data published by Paine in 1966 were partly fabricated or misinterpreted
That the mussel mat itself shelters more than three hundred other species, which raises the total diversity of the system
That the mussel ends up being crowded out by Pisaster after all on the untouched control plot
That no measurable effect on species diversity was ever actually established
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 2016 reanalysis shows that the mussel bed shelters more than three hundred associated species in its gaps: the diversity of the bare substrate drops, but the total diversity goes up.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When and in what context does Robert Paine coin the term “keystone species”?
choix: In 1963, when he designs the experiment, as a working hypothesis
In 1966, in the same article that reports the drop from fifteen to eight species
In 1969, in a three-page note published in the same journal
The term was coined later by another ecologist working on wolves
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1969, in a three-page note published in The American Naturalist, Paine proposes the term “keystone,” in reference to the central stone of an arch whose removal brings everything down.
